entities.summary:
The Ming dynasty (1368–1644) was the last Han Chinese imperial dynasty, ruling one of the largest and most powerful nations in the world. Founded by Zhu Yuanzhang (the Hongwu Emperor) after overthrowing the Mongol Yuan dynasty, the Ming restored Han Chinese rule and presided over some of China's greatest architectural, literary, and exploratory achievements.

The Yongle Emperor's construction of the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406-1420) created the world's largest palace complex. Zheng He's seven naval expeditions (1405-1433) sent fleets of over 300 ships and 28,000 men to Southeast Asia, South Asia, Arabia, and East Africa — voyages far exceeding European exploration of the same era. China's decision to halt these expeditions and focus inward rather than colonizing has been called one of history's most consequential strategic choices.

The Great Wall's most recognized sections were built or restored during the Ming period. The Wanli Emperor's reign saw the printing of the Yongle Dadian encyclopedia (22,877 volumes) and the development of porcelain, silk, and lacquerware exported globally through trade. The dynasty fell in 1644 when rebel Li Zicheng captured Beijing and the last Ming emperor committed suicide, with the Manchu Qing dynasty filling the power vacuum.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Ming dynasty's decision to halt Zheng He's global voyages — forgoing a potential Chinese maritime empire — is one of history's great counterfactual turning points, as Europe instead built its colonial empires in the same era.
